steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on joint learning of blind super-resolution and crack segmentation for degraded inspection images. Explain why real-world crack segmentation is hard and list the contributions of our framework.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Automatic inspection of infrastructure; focus on camera-based crack segmentation
- Why crack segmentation is hard: four problems
- Our unified framework and its four contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Inspection
  - many constructions/infrastructures (buildings, pavements, bridges, tunnels) dilapidated; hard to always inspect all manually
  - automatic inspection: prospective solution for efficient diagnosis
  - sensors: Falling Weight Deflectometer, Pavement Density Profiler, Ground Penetrating Radar
  - this paper: crack segmentation on images from generic cameras for visual inspection
- Crack segmentation
  - binary semantic segmentation (cite); two classes, much fewer than generic multiclass segmentation (cite)
  - still not easy even with powerful deep networks, because:
  - \langle A \rangle high class-imbalance: far fewer crack pixels than background (Fig. 1 (b)); all pixels tend to be classified to background
  - \langle B \rangle fine cracks: hairline, hard to segment (Fig. 1 (b))
  - \langle C \rangle low-resolution (LR): tunnels (cite), pavements (cite); camera cannot get close for safety (Fig. 1 (a))
  - \langle D \rangle blurred images: captured from moving vehicles (cars, drones) (Fig. 1 (a))
  - combination of all -> challenging even with SoTA (Fig. 1 (c), (d))
- Contributions (Table I)
  - 1. CSBSR: like CSSR from our earlier conference paper (cite), SR network accepting LR image in series with segmentation network, end-to-end joint learning; extended with blind SR for realistically-blurred images; optimizes SR for segmentation (Fig. 1 (e)) more than similar methods with non-blind SR (cite) (Fig. 1 (c), (d))
  - 2. Boundary Combo (BC) loss: fine boundaries evaluated locally with global constraints; robust to class imbalance
  - 3. Segmentation-aware SR-loss weights: SR network less optimized due to gradient vanishing through segmentation network; BC loss weights SR loss; extra weights from fine-crack and hard-negative pixels
  - 4. Blur skip: blur left in imperfect SR image hurts segmentation; estimated blur passed to segmentation network via skip connection

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many constructions and infrastructures in the world, such as buildings, pavements, bridges and tunnels, are dilapidated, and it is difficult to always inspect all of them manually. Automatic inspection is one of the prospective solutions for diagnosing these constructions efficiently instead of manual inspection. This kind of inspection can be done with several types of sensors, such as the Falling Weight Deflectometer, the Pavement Density Profiler and the Ground Penetrating Radar, but this paper focuses on crack segmentation on images taken by generic cameras for visual inspection.

In computer vision, crack segmentation is defined as binary semantic segmentation. The number of classes in crack segmentation (two classes) is much fewer than in recent generic multiclass segmentation, but real-world crack segmentation is still not an easy problem even with the recent powerful deep neural networks. The reasons are the following:

- \langle A \rangle. High class-imbalance: There are much fewer crack pixels than non-crack pixels (background pixels), as shown in Fig. 1 (b). In this kind of problem all pixels tend to be classified to background.

- \langle B \rangle. Fine cracks: Cracks can be hairline, and those are difficult to segment, as shown in Fig. 1 (b).

- \langle C \rangle. Low-Resolution (LR): When inspecting various structures such as tunnels and pavements, the inspection camera captures cracks in LR (as shown in Fig. 1 (a)) because it cannot get close to the structures for safety reasons.

- \langle D \rangle. Cracks in blurred images: Inspection images are usually taken from moving vehicles such as cars and drones so that inspection is efficient, so the images can be blurred, as shown in Fig. 1 (a).

Each of these problems is already not easy, and crack segmentation is even more challenging because all of them are combined, even with SoTA methods, as shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). To deal with these problems, this paper proposes a unified framework with the following novel contributions (Table I):

- 1. Crack Segmentation with Blind Super-Resolution (CSBSR): Like Crack Segmentation with Super Resolution (CSSR), which we proposed in our earlier conference paper, the CSBSR proposed here connects "a network for SR accepting an input LR image" in series to "a segmentation network" for end-to-end joint learning. We extend CSSR to CSBSR with blind SR so that it can handle realistically-blurred images. Joint learning of blind SR and segmentation lets us optimize SR to improve segmentation (Fig. 1 (e)) more than similar methods that use non-blind SR and segmentation (Fig. 1 (c) and (d)).

- 2. Boundary Combo (BC) loss for segmentation: Besides super-resolving tiny cracks as described above, fine boundaries are evaluated locally with global constraints in the whole image, so that fine cracks are detected robustly to the class-imbalance problem.

- 3. Segmentation-aware SR-loss weights: CSSR and CSBSR use BC loss to train the segmentation network and also the SR network end-to-end, but the SR network is less optimized because of gradient vanishing through the segmentation network. To train the SR network more for segmentation, BC loss directly weights a loss for SR. To improve further, the SR loss is also weighted by additional weights based on fine-crack and hard-negative pixels.

- 4. Blur skip for blur-reflected task learning: An SR image is imperfect, so the blur effects that remain in it have a negative impact on segmentation. To make segmentation more robust to the blur effects, the blur estimated in SR is given to the segmentation network through a skip connection.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
While many constructions and infrastructures such as buildings, pavements, bridges, and tunnels are dilapidated in the world, it is difficult to always inspect all of them manually. Instead of manual inspection, automatic inspection is one of the prospective solutions for efficiently diagnosing these constructions. While such inspection can be achieved with several types of sensors, such as the Falling Weight Deflectometer, the Pavement Density Profiler, and the Ground Penetrating Radar, this paper focuses on crack segmentation on images captured by generic cameras for visual inspection.

Crack segmentation [1] is defined as binary semantic segmentation in the field of computer vision. While the number of classes in crack segmentation (i.e., two classes) is much fewer than in recent generic multiclass segmentation [2,3,4], real-world crack segmentation is not an easy problem even with recent powerful deep neural networks, for the following reasons:

- \langle A \rangle. High class-imbalance: The number of crack pixels is much less than the number of non-crack pixels (i.e., background pixels), as shown in Fig. 1 (b). In such a problem, all pixels tend to be classified to background.

- \langle B \rangle. Fine cracks: Cracks can be hairline, which makes them difficult to segment, as shown in Fig. 1 (b).

- \langle C \rangle. Low-Resolution (LR): For inspection of various structures such as tunnels [5] and pavements [6], an inspection camera captures cracks in LR (as shown in Fig. 1 (a)) because it cannot get close to the structures for safety reasons.

- \langle D \rangle. Cracks in blurred images: Since inspection images are usually captured from moving vehicles such as cars and drones for efficient inspection, those images can be blurred, as shown in Fig. 1 (a).

While each of these problems is already not easy, crack segmentation is more challenging due to the combination of all of them, even with SoTA methods, as shown in Fig. 1 (c) and (d). To cope with these problems, this paper proposes a unified framework consisting of the following novel contributions (Table I):

- 1. Crack Segmentation with Blind Super-Resolution (CSBSR): As with Crack Segmentation with Super Resolution (CSSR) proposed in our earlier conference paper [7], the CSBSR proposed in this paper connects "a network for SR accepting an input LR image" in series to "a segmentation network" for end-to-end joint learning. We extend CSSR to CSBSR with blind SR to handle realistically-blurred images. Our joint learning of blind SR and segmentation allows us to optimize SR for improving segmentation (Fig. 1 (e)) more than similar methods [8,9] that use non-blind SR and segmentation (Fig. 1 (c) and (d)).

- 2. Boundary Combo (BC) loss for segmentation: In addition to super-resolving tiny cracks as mentioned above, fine boundaries are locally evaluated with global constraints in the whole image in order to detect fine cracks robustly to the class-imbalance problem.

- 3. Segmentation-aware SR-loss weights: While CSSR and CSBSR use BC loss to train not only the segmentation network but also the SR network in an end-to-end manner, the SR network is less optimized due to gradient vanishing through the segmentation network. To train the SR network more for segmentation, BC loss directly weights a loss for SR. For further improvement, the SR loss is also weighted by additional weights based on fine-crack and hard-negative pixels.

- 4. Blur skip for blur-reflected task learning: Since an SR image is imperfect, the blur effects remaining in it have a negative impact on segmentation. To make segmentation more robust to the blur effects, the blur estimated in SR is provided to the segmentation network via a skip connection.

References:
[1] F. Elghaish, S. Talebi, E. Abdellatef, S. T. Matarneh, M. R. Hosseini, S. Wu, M. Mayouf, A. Hajirasouli et al. , “Developing a new deep learning cnn model to detect and classify highway cracks,” Journal of Engineering, Design and Technology , 2021.
[2] E. Shelhamer, J. Long, and T. Darrell, “Fully convolutional networks for semantic segmentation,” IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. , vol. 39, no. 4, pp. 640–651, 2017.
[3] K. He, G. Gkioxari, P. Dollár, and R. B. Girshick, “Mask R-CNN,” IEEE Trans. Pattern Anal. Mach. Intell. , vol. 42, no. 2, pp. 386–397, 2020.
[4] A. Kirillov, K. He, R. B. Girshick, C. Rother, and P. Dollár, “Panoptic segmentation,” in CVPR , 2019.
[5] S. Stent, R. Gherardi, B. Stenger, K. Soga, and R. Cipolla, “An image-based system for change detection on tunnel linings,” in MVA , 2013.
[6] Y. Fei, K. C. P. Wang, A. Zhang, C. Chen, J. Q. Li, Y. Liu, G. Yang, and B. Li, “Pixel-level cracking detection on 3d asphalt pavement images through deep-learning- based cracknet-v,” IEEE Trans. Intell. Transp. Syst. , vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 273–284, 2020.
[7] Y. Kondo and N. Ukita, “Crack segmentation for low-resolution images using joint learning with super-resolution,” in MVA , 2021.
[8] H. Bae, K. Jang, and Y.-K. An, “Deep super resolution crack network (srcnet) for improving computer vision–based automated crack detectability in in situ bridges,” Structural Health Monitoring , vol. 20, no. 4, pp. 1428–1442, 2021.
[9] L. Wang, D. Li, Y. Zhu, L. Tian, and Y. Shan, “Dual super-resolution learning for semantic segmentation,” in CVPR , 2020, https://github.com/Dootmaan/DSRL .
